_comment: The beaches this forecaster is for, on the Coronado peninsula, all sharing
one offshore buoy (46232) and one blocking geometry.
CORONADO IS NOT ONE BEACH. It is carried here as three digitised break
segments, because the window varies along its own length by nearly as much
as it varies between the named beaches. The west edge of the swell window
IS the bearing to the Point Loma tip, and that bearing sweeps as you walk
the sand: measured, 241.9 degrees at the north break to 260.1 at the south,
giving 41.3 / 47.6 / 54.9 degrees of open window across 2.8 km. For scale,
the whole Breakers-to-Gator spread is 23.1 to 62.2. A single number for
'Coronado' averages across a 13.6-degree spread and is wrong at both ends.
WHAT MATTERS IN THESE COORDINATES, measured rather than assumed:
POSITION sets the window. Both edges of the swell-side window are
blocker-derived (Point Loma west, Coronado Islands east), so the seaward
half-plane clip never binds there. Moving a break 500 m north costs
Coronado about 4.4 degrees of window.
THE SHORELINE CHORD DOES NOT set the window. Rotating it plus or minus
10 degrees moves the swell-side window by exactly zero at all three
beaches; it moves only the near-useless south-east arc. An earlier
version of this comment claimed the chord 'matters most' and that five
degrees of chord error moved the window five degrees. That was never
measured and it is false. See tests/test_geometry.py.
The chord still earns its place: it sets the seaward normal, which is
what the headline 'shadow edge sits one degree off the shore normal'
claim is computed from, and what wind fetch and refraction will need.
It is simply not the thing that decides which swell arrives.
THE POINT LOMA TIP carries the west edge for every spot in this file.
100 m of tip error moves that edge about 1 degree. It is NOT one point:
charted 2026-09-22, it is a rounded headland whose tangent lands on a
different vertex for each break, so the blocker carries an `outline`
and each break takes its own edge off it.
`position` is OPTIONAL and derived from the shoreline midpoint when
omitted. It is written out only for the un-digitised spots, which predate
this file and whose stored position sits 698 m off its own chord - exactly
the drift that duplicating a derivable value invites. Do not add it back
for a digitised break.
Blockers are listed separately. `continues` says the landmass carries on
past that endpoint rather than ending there, which is how a peninsula
differs from an island.

spots.name: Coronado Central Beach — north break

provenance.method: chord endpoints are the NOAA ENC harbour-band (enc_harbour/84) coastline vertices nearest the 2026-09-14 Google Earth trace, via collector.shoreline region=coronado
provenance.note: The chart says where the COAST is; it cannot say where along it the BREAK is, so the alongshore location is still the one chosen by hand on 2026-09-14 and only the coordinates are charted. Replaced trace (32.6866337, -117.1975652) / (32.6855447, -117.1918651); endpoints moved 23.9 m and 38.1 m. No loose line ends within 300 m of either endpoint on this band, so neither can be a chart gap (the Point Loma harbour-band fault, BRIEFING §26). A chart coastline is generalised and referenced to a tidal datum, not a waterline on the day of an image: expect offsets of tens of metres against any trace and do not read them as error.

spots.notes: Northernmost of the three, closest to Point Loma, so the most shadowed: west window 41.3 degrees, cut off at 241.9. Also 164.6-187.4 to the south and a 192.6-198.6 channel between the islands.

spots.notes: North Island's ocean shore. Closest of all spots to Point Loma, so expected to be the most shadowed. Zuniga Jetty is a missing blocker here - see blockers._missing. COORDINATES STILL ESTIMATED, not digitised; out of scope for now by decision, not because they are good.

blockers.name: Point Loma peninsula

provenance.method: per-break tangent to the charted tip, NOAA ENC approach band (enc_approach/88) via collector.shoreline region=point_loma, read by forecast.blockeredge
provenance.note: Replaced a Google Earth trace of the seaward-most waterline point (32.6648144, -117.2427037, digitised 2026-09-14). The tip is a rounded headland and the breaks see it from bearings 18 degrees apart, so each break's tangent lands on a DIFFERENT charted vertex - up to 330 m apart around the curve - and no single point is right for all of them: the north break's tangent vertex puts the south break's edge 0.41 degrees out, the south break's puts the north's 0.67 out. Hence `outline`: the convex hull of the 218 charted vertices south of 32.672 N (only a hull vertex can ever be a tangent), and geometry takes the edge per break. `a` is the center break's tangent vertex and stands for the tip in any single-point use. Moves against the imagery trace: north -0.53, center +0.01, south +0.17 degrees. The coastal band (enc_coastal/70) agrees to within 0.25 degrees on every Coronado break. The harbour band (enc_harbour/84) is finer but its coastline has a 336 m HOLE at the tip (part 19 ends at 32.66539, -117.24137; the next line starts at 32.66663, -117.24464), presumably carried by another layer such as shoreline construction; its south-break tangent sits on that line end and is not used. `b` is the northernmost ocean-side charted vertex in the extract, at Ocean Beach; it only says the ridge runs north and does not end, and it is clipped by the query envelope, not by the coast.

blockers.notes: The tip is `outline`, with `a` as its representative vertex; the ridge runs north from there and does not end, so everything past `b` is land too. The tip carries the west edge of every spot in this file, per break, at about 1 degree per 100 m.

blockers.name: Coronado Islands (South group)

provenance.method: extreme-bearing vertices of the southern island group, NOAA ENC approach band
provenance.note: Charted 2026-09-20 from NOAA's ENC approach band (enc_approach/88) via collector.shoreline region=baja, endpoints read by forecast.blockeredge. The coastal band (enc_coastal/70) agrees to within 0.05 degrees on every edge. Two candidate vertices existed for one endpoint of each island and they differ by at most 0.044 degrees; the wider-shadow pick was taken. 4459 m across at 29.4 km, Fresnel about 1.9 at 15 s, which is the low end of the 1.9 to 5.4 range BRIEFING section 10 measured. At a 0.3 km link distance this group resolves further into three islands separated by 0.98 and 0.25 degrees, but those sub-degree gaps move with the link distance and the two-cluster split does not - it is identical from 0.3 km to 3 km on both chart bands.

blockers.notes: Three islands close together; treated as one because their gaps are sub-degree and not stable under the clustering distance.

blockers.name: Coronado Islands (North group)

provenance.method: extreme-bearing vertices of the northern island, NOAA ENC approach band
provenance.note: Charted 2026-09-20 from NOAA's ENC approach band (enc_approach/88) via collector.shoreline region=baja, endpoints read by forecast.blockeredge. The coastal band (enc_coastal/70) agrees to within 0.05 degrees on every edge. Two candidate vertices existed for one endpoint of each island and they differ by at most 0.044 degrees; the wider-shadow pick was taken. This island is 1427 m across at 28.2 km, giving a Fresnel number of about 0.2 at 15 s - its shadow is very largely filled by diffraction and the hard edge here is close to fiction. Its HIGH-bearing edge is the low edge of the west swell window on every break, so the number is load-bearing even though the shadow is soft.

blockers.notes: Island, not a peninsula: the shadow closes on both sides.

blockers.name: Baja peninsula

provenance.method: seaward-most charted vertex of the Mexican coast as seen from Coronado, NOAA ENC approach band (enc_approach/88), read by forecast.blockeredge
provenance.note: `a` is a TANGENT, not the end of a chord. The Baja coast is seen almost exactly edge-on from these breaks - every charted vertex from the border to the extract's southern limit spans 147 to 168 degrees - so one vertex carries the whole edge, the same geometry as the Point Loma tip. It is a softer problem than Point Loma because it is 23 km out rather than 5: 100 m of error moves the edge 0.25 degrees, against about 1 there. The coastal band agrees to 0.18 degrees. The maximum sits 9.6 km NORTH of the last charted vertex, so the coast turns away inside the data and this is a tangent rather than the chart running out - forecast.blockeredge carries that alarm and it is quiet here.

blockers.notes: The coast running south from the border. `a` is the tangent and carries the southern edge of every Coronado window; `b` only says the land continues past it and does not end. UNTESTED CLAIM: no coast south of 32.3834 - where NOAA's charts stop - bears higher than `a` from these breaks. Public landmark positions put Punta Descanso, Ensenada, Punta Banda and Punta Eugenia at 152 to 159 degrees, all below it, but those are typed estimates and not a measurement. GSHHG or a Mexican chart would settle it.

_missing: Zuniga Jetty and the harbour-entrance shoal, which matter for Breakers Beach and probably narrow its window further. Not included because inventing coordinates for them would put false precision into the one number this module exists to compute.
The shelf itself. This is a geometric blocking model only - it says what is BLOCKED, not what refraction and shoaling do to what gets through.
Digitised coordinates for Breakers and Gator. Scoped out for now; their windows are computed from estimates and are flagged accordingly.
